title: How France’s Jacobin state paved the way for the riots
gist: Marc Le Chevallier argues France's recurring apolitical riots stem from a two-century Jacobin project that stripped out intermediary bodies such as guilds, unions and the Church, leaving an obese, indebted and weak state facing an atomised society. He contrasts Britain's cooperation with religious institutions and warns that nearly all French parties, from RN to LFI, offer only more state, implying a bleak political outlook.

insights.claim: Le Chevallier argues that after years of centralisation France's Jacobin state is obese, indebted and weak, unable to pacify the atomised society it helped create.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: Structural fiscal strain and weak state capacity in France are relevant to French sovereign risk.
insights.quote: France has a Jacobin state that, after years of centralisation, is obese, indebted and weak

insights.claim: Macron's responses to crises have almost always meant more state, including 'whatever it costs' pandemic spending, the energy price shield and 10,000 extra police and gendarmes since 2017.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: Ratchet of state spending underpins France's fiscal deficit trajectory.

insights.claim: Macron dismantled traditional parties, limited engagement with trade unions and eroded local government autonomy, which the author calls the pinnacle of a toxic arrangement.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: Weakened intermediary channels raise the risk of disorderly protest over reforms.

insights.claim: Without intermediary bodies, France developed a tradition of top-down state coercion through bureaucracy and riot police, met by bottom-up resistance through strikes and barricades.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: Explains France's structurally high strike and protest risk.

insights.claim: Under de Gaulle a strong state and strong civil society coexisted in a precarious equilibrium, which unravelled after the 1968 cultural revolution and later economic and technological change including social media.

insights.claim: Thick institutions such as trade unions, the Church and national parties have massively dwindled across the West, but France lacked institutional antibodies to slow the decline.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: France is more exposed than peers to institutional hollowing-out.
insights.locator: All Western societies have been affected.

insights.claim: Le Chevallier argues that France's tradition of unrest is old but its culture of rioting is new, with riots breaking out on Bastille Day, New Year's Eve, Halloween or after PSG wins, amplified by social media.

insights.so_what: Riot risk is now event-driven and less predictable from political triggers.

insights.claim: Unlike in 1830 and 1848, when looting was constrained or punished by insurgents themselves, today's pillaging reflects rioting as a pleasurable transgressive experience.

insights.so_what: Loss of internal norms makes disorder harder to contain.

insights.claim: Most 2023 rioters came from the banlieues, and the author argues the Jacobin model compounds immigrant uprooting by asking communities to privatise intermediary bodies such as religion, offering an abstract civic identity with little appeal.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: Integration failure is a structural driver of French social risk.

insights.claim: In 2023, imams' calls for calm reportedly had little effect, and in some cases peace was said to have been restored by local gangs for whom riots were bad for business.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: Informal power structures can matter more than official ones in restoring order.

insights.claim: In Bradford in 2007, collaboration between police and local mosques led to a 30 per cent fall in criminal damage during Ramadan, illustrating Britain's model of working with religious institutions.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: Evidence that partnering with community institutions reduces disorder.

insights.claim: Despite its own integration crisis and higher inequality, Britain has largely avoided France's regular bouts of anarchic, apolitical rioting because of its willingness to work with non-state institutions.

insights.claim: Le Chevallier predicts a bleak political future because most French parties, from the RN to LFI, sit in the Jacobin tradition and offer only more state: more tax on the left, more repressive powers on the right.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: Whichever side wins, expect higher taxes or more state intervention, not structural reform.
insights.quote: Their solutions always involve expanding the state: more tax on the left or more repressive powers on the right.

insights.claim: The author concludes that in attempting to build Hobbes's Leviathan, France has ended up in his state of nature.
insights.speaker: Marc Le Chevallier
insights.so_what: Summarises a structural rather than cyclical view of French instability.
insights.quote: In attempting to create Hobbes’s Leviathan, France has ended up in his state of nature.
